items.e: [With regard to the presentation of] the blood from any of the sacrifices on the outer altar: as long as one makes one presentation of blood, atonement is generated. Even with regard to a sin-offering, one presentation is of fundamental importance. Making the remaining [three of] the four [required] presentations is [merely] the optimum manner of fulfilling the mitzvah, as [implied by Deuteronomy 12:27]: "The blood of your sacrifices shall you pour on the altar." [One can infer that one] pouring of blood on the altar is of fundamental importance.
Whenever [a priest] poured [blood] over the altar when he should have cast it upon it, the obligation is fulfilled, as [implied by the verse:] "The blood of your sacrifices shall you pour."

With regard to all of the blood presented on the inner altar, if one of the presentations is lacking, the sacrifice does not bring atonement. Instead, all of them are integral for the atonement, for Scripture was precise with regard to their number, as [Leviticus 4:7, 17; 16:14] states: "seven times."
If the owner died after one of the presentations of the blood of a sin-offering was made, the remainder of the presentations should be made after his death.
If, however, he made one presentation during the day, he should not make the [remaining] three at night.

If one made one [of the presentations of blood required to be made on] the inner altar on [that altar] and made the remainder on the outer [altar], he is liable for [ karet ] for offering [a sacrifice] outside its appropriate place.
If [a priest] was sprinkling [the blood of a sacrifice on the altar] and his hand was cut off before the blood reached the space above the altar, the sprinkling of the blood is not acceptable.

If one changed [the order] of corners [of the altar on which the blood was presented when bringing] a sin-offering - whether for a sin-offering [whose blood] is offered on the inner altar or a sin-offering [whose blood] is offered on the outer altar - [the sacrifice] is disqualified. If, however, [the order of the presentation of the blood] for other sacrifices is changed, [the sacrifices] are acceptable.

If [the priest] presented the blood beyond the corner of the altar - whether for a sin-offering or for another offering and whether for the inner altar or for the outer altar - [the sacrifice] is unacceptable.

When blood that according to [the Torah's] command should have been presented above the midpoint of the altar was presented below it; if according to [the Torah's] command, it should have been presented below the midpoint of the altar, but it was presented above it; if [blood that] according to [the Torah's] command should have been presented inside [the Temple] and was presented on the outer altar; if [blood that] should have been presented on the outer altar was presented in [the Temple]; or if blood that should have been presented on the outer [altar] was presented on the ramp in a place that is not opposite the foundation [of the altar], [in all these instances,] the meat of the sacrifice is unacceptable. Nevertheless, the owners of the sacrifices receive atonement because of it, for its blood has reached the altar. Although it did not reach the proper place, it is as if it reached its [proper] place with regard to atonement. When does the above apply? When the person casting [the blood] is acceptable for Temple service. If, however, a person fit for Temple service received [the blood] and gave it to a person who is unacceptable and that unacceptable person presented [blood] that should have been presented above [the midpoint] of the altar below its midpoint, [blood] that should have been presented [on the] outer [altar] was presented inside [the Temple Sanctuary], [blood] that should have been presented inside [the Temple Sanctuary] was presented[on the] outer [altar], or one presented [the blood] on the ramp in a place that is not opposite the foundation [of the altar], the meat of the sacrifice is not disqualified if [any of the sacrificial animal's] blood of life remains. Instead, an acceptable person should receive the remainder of the blood of life and cast it [on the altar] in its appropriate place.

[The following rules apply when] the blood of sacrificial animals becomes mixed between two types of blood or between two cups of blood. If [the blood of sacrifices that require] one presentation [of blood] was mixed with [the blood of others that require] one presentation [of blood], one presentation should be made of the entire [mixture]. Similarly, if [the blood of sacrifices that require] four presentations [of blood was mixed] with [the blood of others that require] four presentations, four presentations should be made of the entire [mixture]. If, [however, the blood of sacrifices that require] one presentation [of blood] was mixed with [the blood of others that require] two presentations that are four, one presentation should be made of the entire [mixture]. If [blood that was] to be presented on the upper [half of the altar] became mixed with [blood that was] to be presented on the lower [half of the altar], all [the blood] should be poured into the [waste] channel and the sacrifices are disqualified. Even if the remainder of [the blood from] a sin-offering is mixed with the blood of a burnt-offering in which instance, all of the blood should be presented on the bottom of the altar, the entire [mixture] should be poured into the [waste] channel.

If [blood from a sin-offering became mixed with the remnants of the blood of a burnt-offering] and [the priest] did not inquire [concerning the law], but instead presented some of the mixture on the upper portion [of the altar] and some on the lower portion, it is acceptable. If he presented a portion on the upper [portion of the altar] and then inquired, he should present [the remainder] on the lower portion. He is considered to have fulfilled his obligation for both [sacrifices].

If blood that was required to be presented in the Temple building became mixed with blood to be presented on the outer [altar], the entire [mixture] should be poured into the [waste] channel. If he did not inquire and took the mixture of the blood and presented some in the Temple [building] and some outside - whether first he presented it inside and then he presented it outside or first he presented it outside and then he presented it inside - everything is acceptable. When does the above apply? With regard to the blood [of the sacrifices that must] be presented on the outer [altar] with the exception of a sin-offering. If, however, the blood of a sin-offering that should be presented outside becomes mixed with the blood of a sin-offering that should be presented inside, it is acceptable [only] if one made the presentation outside and then made the presentation inside. If, however, one made the presentation inside and then made the presentation outside, [the sacrifice whose blood was to be presented outside] is unacceptable. [The rationale is that] the blood of a sin-offering that was brought into the Temple building - even the blood of a sin-offering brought by an individual [whose meat] should be eaten - becomes forbidden, as [implied by Leviticus 6:23]: "Any sin-offering whose blood has been brought [into the Tent of Meeting... shall not be eaten]." [The above applies] provided [the blood] is brought in through the gate to the Temple Building, for the prooftext speaks of it being "brought," implying an ordinary manner of entrance. If, however, it was brought in through a wicket or through a window or the roof, it is not disqualified.

When the blood from a bull brought [because of the violation of a law] forgotten [by the High Court] or from a goat brought [because of the violation of the prohibition against] idol worship which should be brought into the Sanctuary was brought to the Holy of Holies, it is disqualified. For this place is inward with regard to the appropriate place for this blood. Similarly, with regard to the bull and the goat brought on Yom Kippur whose blood is brought into the Holy of Holies, if the blood [of these offerings] was brought into the Holy of Holies and sprinkled there, was then taken to the Sanctuary and afterwards, returned to the Holy of Holies, it is disqualified. [The High Priest] should not complete the sprinkling [of the blood] in the Holy of Holies. Once he departs, he has departed. Similarly, if he completed the sprinklings in the Holy of Holies, then brought the blood into the Sanctuary and made some of the sprinklings [required there], then took [the blood] out of the Sanctuary and afterwards returned it, he should not complete the sprinklings in the Sanctuary. [The rationale is that] since the blood was taken out of its place, it became disqualified.

If the blood of an [ordinary] sin-offering was received in two cups and one of them was taken outside, the one that remained inside is acceptable and the sprinklings may be performed. If, [by contrast,] one [of the cups] was taken into the Sanctuary and sprinkled there, even the one left outside is disqualified, as [implied by the prooftext] : "whose blood has been brought in," i.e., even if only a portion of its blood was brought in to the Sanctuary to bring about atonement, it is disqualified.

[The following rules apply when] the blood of an [ordinary] sin-offering was taken into [the Sanctuary] to achieve atonement, but nothing was done and instead, he took it out without sprinkling it inside. If he brought it in unknowingly, [the blood] remains acceptable and should be sprinkled outside, for nothing to achieve atonement was done in the Sanctuary. If he brought it in intentionally, it is disqualified.

If the sin-offering itself was brought into the Sanctuary, it is acceptable, because [the prooftext] mentions "whose blood was brought in," [i.e., it is the blood] and not the meat [that disqualifies it].
When a sin-offering of a fowl moved in its death throes and entered the Sanctuary, it is acceptable.
If the blood of a sin-offering of a fowl was taken into the Sanctuary in its neck, there is an unresolved doubt whether its neck is considered a receptacle [which would disqualify the sacrifice].

If the blood of a sin-offering of a fowl was spilled and then collected, there is an unresolved question: Does the receptacle disqualify the blood or not? Therefore the fowl should be burnt like all the sin-offerings of fowl concerning which there are unresolved doubts.

When [a priest] received the blood of a sin-offering in four cups and made one presentation [on the altar] from each cup, the remainder of all four cups is poured on the altar's base, as [Leviticus 4:30] states: "And all of its blood shall be poured [on the base of the altar]." If he made all four presentations from one cup, the remnants of that cup should be poured on the altar's base and the other cups poured in the drainage canal.

When blood falls into water or into ordinary blood, it should not be sprinkled on the altar. If it was sprinkled, it is disqualified. When water fell into blood in a receptacle, if it has the appearance of blood, it is acceptable. If wine or ordinary blood fell into it, we make an assessment [as follows]: Were it to have been water would there have been enough to nullify the blood in the receptacle to the extent that it would no longer have the appearance of blood, he should not sprinkle from [the mixture]. If there would not have been enough to nullify its appearance, he should sprinkle from it.

When the blood of sacrificial animals becomes mixed with the blood of animals that are disqualified from the altar or with the blood of sacrificial animals that were disqualified because of unsatisfactory ritual slaughter, the entire mixture should be poured into the drainage canal. Even if all the cups [of blood] were offered aside from one, it should be poured into the drainage canal and all of those offerings are unacceptable. If the [life-]blood [of a sacrificial animal] became mixed with blood concentrated [in the limbs], [the mixture] should be poured into the drainage canal. If, [however,] one did not ask and presented [the blood on the altar], [the sacrifice] is acceptable.

If one cast the organs and fats offered on the altar, the limbs of burnt-offerings, the handfuls [of meal offered on the altar], the frankincense, or the meal-offerings that are to be burnt on the [altar's] pyre after they were consecrated in a sacred utensil, whether by hand or with a utensil, whether with one's right hand or with one's left hand, they are acceptable.

When wine or water was poured [on the altar as a libation] with a bowl, the hin measure, or another sacred utensil, it is acceptable. If they were poured with an ordinary vessel or by hand, they are unacceptable.

When one arranged the limbs [of a burnt-offering] or the handful [of meal from a meal-offering] and then arranged the logs for the altar's pyre above them or arranged them at the side of the limbs, there is an unresolved doubt whether this is considered as the typical way of having them consumed by fire or not. Therefore as an initial preference, one should not offer them in this manner, but if one did, it is acceptable.
